supplement.holds: Survey instruments, full learning texts, and the grading instrument. The document does not say it holds statistics; all similarity, lexical-diversity and quality estimates with SEs are in this PDF (Tables 5, 6, A5, A6; appendices A-C).

paper_design_summary: Middlebury undergraduates in proctored lab sessions were randomly assigned (lab per time slot, seat per student) to an AI-allowed condition with a logged-in ChatGPT (GPT-4o) account or an AI-forbidden condition; both groups read about an unfamiliar technical topic and wrote an approximately 500-word analytical essay within a 35-minute learning phase, then took a test. About one week later all students wrote a second essay on the same topic (other prompt) and took a test without AI. Essays were scored for quality by Prolific graders and Claude, and for linguistic features including within-group embedding similarity (homogeneity), similarity to the reading, and lexical diversity.

studies.label: Two-session lab experiment: analytical essay with or without generative AI (Session One) and unaided essay one week later (Session Two)

assignment.what_was_assigned: AI-allowed (explicit permission to use any generative AI tool plus a logged-in ChatGPT GPT-4o account) versus AI-forbidden (explicit prohibition; Google, Wikipedia and library tabs) during the Session One learning phase. Topic (3) and essay prompt order were also randomized.
assignment.quote: For each time slot, we randomly assign one lab to the AI-allowed condition and the other to the AI-forbidden condition. We randomly assign each student who signed up for a time slot to a specific computer in one of these two labs.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.1 (Overview); strata = eight Session One time slots, p. 11 Section 3.3

arms.name: AI-allowed
arms.description: Permitted to use any generative AI tool during the 35-minute learning phase; browser preloaded with a dedicated ChatGPT (GPT-4o) account, Wikipedia and the Middlebury library site. Tests taken without AI.

arms.name: AI-forbidden
arms.description: Prohibited from using generative AI; browser preloaded with Google, Wikipedia and the Middlebury library site.

participants.exclusions: 256 sign-ups are balanced by assignment in Table 2 (126 AI-forbidden, 130 AI-allowed; p. 36). 211 attended Session One (82.5 vs 82.3 percent by arm; control N = 104 in Tables 3-6, AI-allowed N = 107 in Table A1). 204 attended both sessions (control 102). Essay analyses use fewer: Session One similarity/style N = 210 (Table 5) or 209 (Table A5), quality N = 209 (Table 6); Session Two similarity/style N = 199 (control 99), quality N = 197 (control 97). Reasons for the missing essays are not stated (Table A5 reports an 'Essay is empty' indicator).
participants.who: Undergraduates at Middlebury College, recruited campus-wide for 'a study on learning' without mention of AI; mean age 20.1, 35.1 percent male, mean GPA 3.68
participants.quote: the 256 students who completed the sign-up survey (column 1), the 211 (82.4 percent) who attended Session One (column 2), and the 204 (79.7 percent) who attended both sessions (column 3)
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 3.2; Table 1 p. 35; Table 2 p. 36

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (GPT-4o), provided logged-in account; any generative AI tool allowed (other tools used by about 2 percent)
ai_tool.how_used: Free use during the learning phase while reading and writing the essay. Logs: 67.3 pp first stage on account use; 57 percent of treated students used it to explain concepts, 31 percent to draft responses, 17 percent to summarize readings (pp. 3, 14; Table 3 p. 37).

task.description: Analytical (expository) essay of about 500 words on an assigned technical topic (blockchain, carbon capture or CRISPR) answering a prompt that asks students to analyze relationships between concepts and support claims with evidence (prompts in Appendix B.2, pp. 69-71). Session Two: second essay on the complementary prompt, written without AI or any resources.
task.duration: Session One: up to 35 minutes for learning and writing combined; Session Two essay: 20 minutes maximum, about one week later (mean 6.99 days)

outcomes.name: Within-group similarity, Session One essays (with AI)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise cosine similarity between a student's essay embedding and all other essays in the same treatment x topic x prompt cell; sentence-embedding model fine-tuned from MPNet. Higher = more similar (less diverse), so the sign is reversed relative to the atlas convention. Also shown in SD units in Figure 6 (p. 32) and Figure A5 (p. 55).

contrasts.reported: Control mean 0.774; ITT 0.001 (0.007); TOT 0.001 (0.010); N = 104 control, 210 total. Text: 'a 0.1 percent change relative to the control mean of 0.774'. Table A5 Panel D repeats the same numbers with N = 209.
contrasts.locator: p. 39, Table 5, Panel C, cols 1-3; p. 17, Section 4.3; p. 65, Table A5, Panel D

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of each essay with all other essays in its treatment x topic x prompt cell
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence-embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) fine-tuned from the MPNet architecture (Song et al., 2020); exact checkpoint not named
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same treatment group, topic and prompt cell (per-student score, then averaged by arm)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Student-level OLS of the per-essay similarity score on assignment with strata fixed effects and double-lasso controls; heteroskedasticity-robust SEs (no adjustment for dependence among scores within a cell)
diversity_detail.notes: Validation (p. 13, fn. 11): within-topic similarity 0.74 vs 0.15 across topics; same prompt 0.78 vs different prompt 0.71.

outcomes.name: Within-group similarity, Session Two essays (unaided, one week later)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same measure as S1-O1, on Session Two essays written without AI or other resources. Higher = more similar (sign reversed relative to the atlas convention).
outcomes.delay: about one week (mean 6.99 days; 61.4 percent exactly seven days), p. 9 fn. 5

contrasts.reported: Control mean 0.762; ITT -0.005 (0.013); TOT -0.007 (0.019); N = 99 control, 199 total.
contrasts.locator: p. 39, Table 5, Panel C, cols 4-6; p. 65, Table A5, Panel D; p. 32, Figure 6

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of each essay with all other essays in its treatment x topic x prompt cell
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence-embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) fine-tuned from MPNet (Song et al., 2020)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each Session Two essay against all other Session Two essays in the same treatment group, topic and prompt cell
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Student-level OLS with strata fixed effects and double-lasso controls; heteroskedasticity-robust SEs
diversity_detail.notes: The text does not discuss this Session Two estimate separately; it is reported only in the tables and figures.

outcomes.name: Overall essay quality, Session One (with AI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Holistic 0-10 overall quality rating, averaged across 3-4 Prolific graders holding a master's or PhD (blind to condition) and then averaged with a Claude Opus 4.8 score on the same rubric. Robustness variant: quality index = mean of five rubric dimensions (accuracy, evidence, relevance, organization, writing style), ITT 0.190 (0.183). Human-only and AI-only overall scores appear in Figure A4 (p. 54). Rating is of analytical quality, not creativity.

contrasts.reported: Overall quality (average): control mean 6.190; ITT 0.246 (0.211); TOT 0.373 (0.321); N = 104 control, 209 total. Text: 0.25 points, 'or 0.17 SD, p = 0.245'. Quality index: control 6.450; ITT 0.190 (0.183); TOT 0.289 (0.279).
contrasts.locator: p. 40, Table 6, Panel B, cols 1-3; p. 18, Section 4.3; benchmark status p. 71, Appendix B.3

outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same rating procedure as S1-O3 (human Prolific graders averaged with Claude Opus 4.8), on Session Two essays. Robustness variant: quality index ITT 0.281 (0.183). Dimension results: writing style 0.411** (0.169), relevance 0.409** (0.198).

company_involvement.description: Funded by Middlebury College's Office of the Provost (p. 1 footnote). The study uses ChatGPT (OpenAI) accounts and Claude Opus (Anthropic) for essay grading and log classification; no company funding, authorship or data role is stated.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1 footnote; p. 8; p. 72 Appendix B.4

eligibility.reason: Students were individually randomized (seat in a lab assigned to a condition within each of eight time slots) to free ChatGPT access versus no AI while writing an analytical essay. The task is not a creative task, but the codebook admits writing tasks whose outputs are compared across writers for similarity; the paper reports within-group embedding similarity of essays (across_people) with 210 students analyzed (104 control), well above 50. Quality ratings are of analytical essay quality, not creativity.

one_line_finding: AI access did not change how similar students' essays were to each other: within-group cosine similarity ITT 0.001 (SE 0.007) on a control mean of 0.774 with AI, and -0.005 (SE 0.013) on a control mean of 0.762 in unaided essays one week later (Table 5, Panel C, p. 39).
open_questions: Scope: the essay is analytical/expository and graded for quality, not creativity. Should the quality outcomes (S1-O3, S1-O4) enter as with_ai/after_ai 'usefulness' records, or should only the similarity outcomes (S1-O1, S1-O2) be kept?
Task type coded 'other' (analytical essay); 'creative_writing' is an alternative if the atlas treats all essays as creative writing.
Session One N for the similarity outcome differs between Table 5 (N = 210, p. 39) and Table A5 (N = 209, p. 65) for identical estimates.

Within-group similarity is computed within treatment x topic x prompt cells, so each student's score depends on the other students' essays in the same cell; SEs are heteroskedasticity-robust at the student level and do not account for this dependence.
Treatment varies by lab within time slot; SEs are not clustered by lab or slot (strata fixed effects only).
Co-authored by the atlas owner (Reyes); the adjudicator may want an independent check.
notes: Main outcomes of the paper are knowledge test scores (Table 4) and essay quality; similarity is a secondary essay feature in Table 5 Panel C. Other essay outcomes not listed because they do not bear on the three questions: Pangram AI-detected fraction, plagiarism fraction, length index, readability index, and the five rubric dimensions (listed in measure_detail of S1-O3/O4). Heterogeneity by automation vs augmentation users (Table 8) covers test score and quality only, not similarity. TOT estimates instrument ChatGPT use with assignment. Session Two essays were written in randomized order with the 10-item test, without AI or any resources; students were not told about Session Two assessments (p. 20 fn. 22).
